stories.headline: Trump Approves Landmark U.S.-Saudi Civilian Nuclear Deal
stories.summary:
President Trump has approved a 30-year agreement allowing Saudi Arabia to develop a civilian nuclear energy program with U.S. assistance, according to senior administration officials. The deal, expected to be formally announced Wednesday, would permit Saudi Arabia to potentially enrich uranium on its own soil at a U.S.-built facility — a provision that goes further than a comparable 2009 U.S. agreement with the United Arab Emirates, which prohibits domestic enrichment.

The arrangement is expected to be worth billions of dollars to American companies involved in building and operating the enrichment infrastructure. Under the terms, if the U.S. objects to domestic enrichment following a joint study, Saudi Arabia would be barred from pursuing it independently or with another foreign partner for 10 years. The deal will be sent to Congress for review, where it is expected to face opposition from some lawmakers on both sides of the aisle.

Nuclear experts and Israeli officials have raised alarm that the agreement could put Saudi Arabia on a path toward developing a nuclear weapon. Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman said in 2018 that if Iran developed a nuclear bomb, Saudi Arabia would 'follow suit as soon as possible.' The deal is not contingent on Saudi-Israeli normalization, departing from the longstanding aspirations of successive U.S. administrations.

The announcement comes amid the ongoing U.S.-Iran conflict, in which preventing Iranian nuclear capability has been cited as a central justification. Critics warn the Saudi deal risks fueling regional nuclear proliferation, while proponents argue it deepens U.S. strategic and commercial ties with a key Gulf partner.

stories.headline: Hegseth Reveals U.S.-Iran War Has Cost $37.5 Billion as Greer Testifies on Trade Agenda
stories.summary:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth disclosed Wednesday before a Senate Appropriations Committee hearing that the U.S. war with Iran has cost at least $37.5 billion — up from the $25 billion figure Pentagon officials provided in late April. CBS News reported the actual total is likely higher. Hegseth clashed sharply with Democratic senators over war strategy and military funding, as the administration simultaneously seeks passage of a record $1.5 trillion defense budget request.

Separately, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer testified before the Senate Finance Committee on President Trump's trade agenda, fielding questions about a new 50 percent tariff imposed on roughly $20 billion in Canadian goods this week. The administration accused Canada of unfair trade practices affecting American autos, dairy, and alcohol. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said he and Trump have agreed to intensify negotiations on a broader trade deal.

Republican senators largely defended the administration's Iran strategy and military spending requests, while Democrats accused Hegseth of failing U.S. troops and lacking a coherent exit strategy. Sen. Gary Peters told Hegseth he had 'failed' service members; Hegseth called the supplemental funding an 'urgent, necessary injection of resources.'

The dual hearings underscore the mounting domestic political pressure on the Trump administration as war costs escalate and trade tensions with a top ally intensify. The national average for a gallon of gasoline has risen to just over $4, up 91 cents from a year ago, as the Iran conflict continues to drive fuel prices higher.

stories.headline: Epstein Modelling Scout Found Dead Near Paris Before Criminal Trial
stories.summary:
Daniel Siad, 69, a modelling scout whose name appeared thousands of times in U.S. government-released Jeffrey Epstein files, was found dead Monday at his home in Colombes, a suburb of Paris. The Nanterre prosecutor's office confirmed the discovery and said an investigation to determine the cause of death has been opened, with an autopsy to be carried out.

Siad had faced multiple complaints in France, including allegations of rape, with the first filed in February 2026. He denied all wrongdoing in recent media interviews, telling BFMTV in May: 'I have never raped anyone in my life.' A BBC investigation published July 18 had featured testimony from an Epstein victim who said Siad introduced her to Epstein and described him as 'essentially a professional trafficker.'

Lawyers representing women who had filed complaints against Siad expressed both anger and grief. 'We are at a loss for words,' they said, accusing the Paris Public Prosecutor's Office of 'scandalous' inaction and saying the delay had denied their clients a criminal trial. One former model who gave a deposition to police in June said Siad's death meant 'an important link in the chain has just vanished into thin air.'

The death comes as scrutiny of Epstein's international network of alleged accomplices remains intense. French authorities had been investigating Epstein's French associates for over a year; the timing of Siad's death — before he could be formally questioned — has drawn sharp criticism from victims' advocates.

stories.headline: Update: NYC Mayor Mamdani Concedes He Cannot Arrest Netanyahu, Urges Federal Action
stories.summary:
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani acknowledged Tuesday that the city does not have legal authority to execute the International Criminal Court arrest warrant against Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, walking back a campaign pledge that had drawn widespread attention. Mamdani called Netanyahu 'a war criminal, the architect of a horrific genocide against the Palestinian people,' and urged U.S. federal authorities to execute the warrant if Netanyahu visits the country later this year.

Mamdani's concession reflects the legal reality that local law enforcement has no jurisdiction over foreign heads of state and cannot enforce international tribunal warrants — authority that rests solely with the federal government. The Trump administration has previously indicated it does not intend to enforce the ICC warrant, which the U.S. has not recognized as binding.

The episode drew criticism from supporters of Israel and from legal experts who noted the original campaign promise was not legally viable. Conservative commentators characterized the reversal as a significant retreat for the new mayor, while progressive supporters of Mamdani argued he was right to continue pressing the federal government on the issue.

Mamdani, who took office earlier this year after a high-profile progressive primary campaign, has made opposition to Israeli military operations in Gaza a prominent feature of his mayoralty. His public statements on Netanyahu are likely to remain a flashpoint in the ongoing national debate over U.S. policy toward Israel.

stories.headline: Update: House Passes War Powers Resolution to Halt Trump's Iran War in Bipartisan Rebuke
stories.summary:
The U.S. House of Representatives voted 215-208 Wednesday to adopt a war powers resolution requiring President Trump to withdraw U.S. forces from Iran or seek formal congressional authorization for the conflict. Four Republicans — Thomas Massie, Brian Fitzpatrick, Tom Barrett, and Warren Davidson — broke with their party to join a united Democratic front, marking the first time a majority of the House has voted to rein in the Iran war, which began in February.

The measure is a concurrent resolution, meaning that if the Senate also passes it, it would not require the president's signature. However, its legal force remains uncertain. The White House dismissed the resolution as unconstitutional, arguing it improperly restricts presidential war powers. The Senate advanced a similar measure in May but has not yet held a full floor vote.

Democrats framed the vote as a significant turning point. Rep. Gregory Meeks, the leading Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, called it "a significant bipartisan rebuke of President Trump's illegal and costly war" and said it signals growing Republican sensitivity to constituent opposition. The vote is the fourth House attempt to limit Trump's war powers and comes amid rising fuel prices, with oil above $90 a barrel, and increasing public skepticism about the conflict's goals.

Republican supporters of the resolution emphasized constitutional principle. Rep. Tom Barrett of Michigan said, "Congress alone declares war — that's something certainly we need to be protective of," adding he was prepared to accept political consequences from Trump for his vote. The vote also comes days after a separate Republican revolt forced the administration to abandon a $1.8 billion fund for political allies, underscoring growing intraparty friction over the Iran campaign.

stories.headline: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang Defends Chinese Open-Source AI, Warns Ban Would Harm U.S.
stories.summary:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang argued Tuesday that American companies should be free to use Chinese open-source AI models, pushing back against a growing campaign in Washington to restrict or ban them. "These Chinese models are excellent," Huang told Axios in an exclusive interview. "Open-source models that are excellent should be used." His comments come as the Trump administration weighs a potential ban on Chinese AI models and as the Chinese model Kimi K3 has drawn fresh attention to Beijing's rapid AI progress.

Huang's stance places the world's leading AI chipmaker in direct tension with policymakers who see Chinese AI as a national security risk. The Trump administration's director of the federal AI testing office resigned recently amid broader tensions over AI policy. Huang contended that restricting access to Chinese models would ultimately disadvantage American companies and innovation rather than protect them.

The intervention is significant given Nvidia's central role in supplying the chips that power AI development globally. The company has previously navigated U.S. export controls limiting sales of advanced chips to China, making Huang's public defense of Chinese AI models a notable departure from the cautious posture many technology executives have adopted on U.S.-China tech competition.

stories.headline: France Becomes First European Country to Ban Under-15s from Social Media
stories.summary:
France's parliament approved a law Tuesday banning children under 15 from social media platforms, making France the first European country to enact such a restriction. Both the Senate and National Assembly adopted the measure, which will require all users in France to verify their age to access social media. President Emmanuel Macron, who championed the legislation, welcomed the vote as a signature policy of his final term in office.

The ban will be implemented in two stages: from September, under-15s will be barred from opening new accounts and age verification will be required for all new users; by January 2027, the rules will apply to existing accounts, meaning every person in France must prove they are 15 or older to use social media. Platforms will be required to use age-verification tools approved by France's privacy regulator.

Critics have raised concerns about privacy risks from mandatory age verification, the ease with which young people may circumvent the ban, and the speed of implementation. Australia enacted a similar ban on under-16s in December, but research by Australia's eSafety Commission found that seven in ten affected children still had some access to the platforms afterward. Experts say France's universal verification requirement may improve compliance but will also heighten privacy exposure.

The law arrives as the UK and European Union develop their own restrictions on minors' access to social media, reflecting a broad Western policy shift driven by growing evidence of harm to children's mental health. France's approach will serve as a closely watched test case for whether age-gating at scale is technically feasible and effective.

stories.headline: Update: India's Modi Government Faces Mounting Pressure as 'Cockroach' Youth Protests Intensify in Delhi
stories.summary:
Pressure on Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government intensified Wednesday as thousands of youth protesters affiliated with the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) maintained a round-the-clock sit-in in central Delhi, demanding education reforms and the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan. The movement gained significant momentum when opposition Congress party leaders, including Rahul Gandhi, staged a surprise march to Modi's residence, demanding resignations of Pradhan, Home Minister Amit Shah, and Modi himself.

The protests escalated after Monday's police crackdown, in which officers used batons and tear gas against tens of thousands of demonstrators who had marched toward parliament as its monsoon session opened. At least 60 people were injured, and Congress shared videos of Gandhi and other MPs being detained and taken to detention centers before being released. Senior opposition figures including former Delhi Chief Minister Arvind Kejriwal and veteran politician Sharad Pawar visited protesters at their base near Jantar Mantar.

The government defended its response. Education Minister Pradhan, in his first comments since the violence, accused Congress of "shamelessly exploiting students as political tools" and said the government had offered a comprehensive discussion but that Congress "chose political spectacle over democratic debate." A federal minister said Gandhi had been informed of the government's willingness to hold talks but alleged he added demands for ministerial resignations, effectively changing the terms.

The protests, driven largely by engineering and civil service exam aspirants frustrated with irregularities and reforms in India's high-stakes national examinations, represent one of the largest sustained youth-led demonstrations India has seen in years. The involvement of major opposition parties has transformed what began as a student movement into a broader political confrontation with the Modi government.
